title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
summary: Keep configuration out of the image, and understand what a Secret really protects.

steps.title: Same image, different config
body: Build one image and run it in dev, test and prod. What differs (URLs, feature flags, connection strings) goes into the cluster, not the image.
A **Secret** looks the same, but its values are **base64-encoded** under `data` (or written as plain text under `stringData`, which the API server encodes for you):

steps.explain: Anyone who can read the Secret object can read the password. base64 is an *encoding* for binary-safe transport, not encryption.

steps.title: What actually protects a Secret
body: base64 hides nothing. What makes Secrets safer than ConfigMaps is everything around them:
- **RBAC**: grant `get` on `secrets` to as few people and service accounts as possible. `list` secrets is effectively "read every password in the namespace".
- **Encryption at rest**: configure the API server to encrypt Secrets in etcd (managed clusters do this, often with a cloud KMS key).
- Kubelets only receive Secrets for pods scheduled on their node, and keep them in memory (tmpfs) when mounted.

- **Do not commit Secret YAML to Git**. Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or an external store (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) synced in by the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver.
kubectl get secret shop-db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
That one-liner is why `get secrets` permission matters.

steps.title: Decode a Secret
prompt: `kubectl get secret -o json` gives you a `data` map of base64 strings. Write `Dictionary<string, string> Decode(Dictionary<string, string> data)` returning the same keys with UTF-8 decoded values.
Then write `string Redact(Dictionary<string, string> decoded)` for logs: each key as `key=***` (keeping only the **length** shown as `key=***(N)`), sorted by key, joined with `", "`.
